Uniform title: Kulasāra Secondary title: Kaulasārasaṃgraha Secondary title: Kulācāranirṇaya
Manuscript: NGMCP 3-251, reel number A 150/16

Description: This manuscript is titled *Kulasāra*, though it is in fact a compilation of fragments from three distinct Kaula treatises. The first is the *Kaulasārasaṃgraha*, which, according to its colophons, is a portion of the *Somabhujavalī*. It begins with chapter 24 and extends through chapter 26. This is followed by the *Kulācāranirṇaya*, which covers chapters 1 to 5. The third fragment is chapter eighteen of a work belonging to the *Śrīvidyā* lineage of Subhagānandanātha; it concerns the funeral rites for a Kaula. These texts, presented in the format of a *tantra*, outline the principles of Kaula ritual and practice. They are typical Kaula works of the later period, dating from after the thirteenth century. Indeed, such texts may be regarded as an independent class of Kaula literature, of which the *Kulārṇavatantra* is one of the earliest representatives.
Notes: Revision 0: December 17, 2013.
Country of Publication: India. oṃ namaḥ śivāyai.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the world, you who are skilled in all branches of knowledge; O All-pervading One, I desire to hear in truth the doctrine of the Kaulikas.
Some sages say this system yields the fruit of the three aims of life (trivarga),
while the best of sages say it bestows all four aims of life (caturvarga).
O Lord, I desire to hear the ritual procedure for that hope in its true essence;
sever this doubt of mine: by what means is this [hope] attained?
The illustrious Lord said:
I shall tell you the essence of the Kula in brief;
O Goddess, this was previously related by me with pleasure in the presence of Brahmā.
Then Brahmā spoke with a focused mind; listen:
"O Devayānī, O Goddess, whenever you were anywhere within the enclosure of the sacrificial altar..."
Then Modaya, seeking the meaning of the mantra for reviving the dead,
gave his own self to him there, O Satvaka, amidst a tumultuous sound.
The middle [state] is the destroyer of the madness of the *yātudhānas* everywhere;
therefore, having abandoned the gods and the asuras, become one whose limit is the Soma, beyond numbering.
From that time forward, a decline in strength arose among the gods;
then, desiring the celestial realm, the gods slew the Dānavas in battle.
Then, out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, I questioned Brahmā:
"O Lord of Gods, by what means might victory belong to the gods?"
Deprived of the Suras and lacking in strength, they have come to this state of existence.
How can there be purification for her? How could her dwelling become pure or new? What is the Kaulika doctrine, and what is this fourfold group of letters?
"You ought to tell me how mortals attain that state.
Brahmā said:
O Lord, having heard in the past that there are indeed four castes,
it is said therein that for every caste, the Brāhmaṇa is called the preceptor.
How could anyone else possibly alter this [account] without me?
He is the teacher of all, the witness, and especially one whose speech is authoritative.
O beloved Girijā, sanctify this mountain with a mantra so that,
by its essence, it may become a source of both worldly enjoyment and liberation for those who are pure.
Or else, by my command, you shall become a Kauśika, O son of a weapon-maker, together with the hosts of Viśvāmitra’s descendants, according to the prescribed rite.
And for all [practitioners], the path to the four aims of life will exist therein;
especially in the Kali Yuga, O Lord of the Kaulas, they shall become vessels for liberation.
O Śaṅkarī, perform the Anuṣṭubh mantra of Śrī Sundarī as the primary one therein;
this is the truth, the truth, again the truth, and the truth indeed, again and again.
"You have established the Kaulika path, which bestows heaven and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is free from passion and falsehood. Thus did the Vedas praise You three times.
The power (śakti) shall consist of the three qualities (triguṇa); hear further concerning that which possesses the three qualities:
having become the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa, they proclaimed it to be the witness of the faults of the manifest world.
The power is expressed as Pradhāna, while Puruṣa is of a nature devoid of qualities;
by his command, we—the Tortoise—[preside over] the creation, maintenance, and destruction [of the world].
She is our supreme power in creation, preservation, and destruction;
she is pleased by the drinking of wine, and by her everything supreme is accomplished.
By that path, there shall be enjoyment and liberation for all;
those who would cast blame upon it will undoubtedly be carried away.
He will effect the release of the seed-fluid from the eyes;
by that, the illustrious practitioner, empowered by the five jewels through recitation, [attains success].
By that [offering], the hosts of gods and asuras go forth satisfied, and Śrī Sundarī is pleased;
all those who know me as Viṣṇuśaraṇa are indeed my father through that substance.
May they be satisfied for all the worlds, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one should cause the ritual of worship to be performed with the causal [mantra] conjoined with Śakti.
Śrīsadaiva said:
Having heard these words of the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
I have fashioned this mantra for the purpose of releasing the seed from the eye.
Therefore, O humans, in the Kaulika doctrine, the group consists of eight.
In this matter, O Goddess, it is fitting that you ask about my birth;
listen, O beloved of my life, as I explain everything else concerning it.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīsomabhujavalī-ākulasārasaṃgraha*.
The Śrī Devī said:
One should first offer water according to the prescribed ritual to Jaddamaladeva;
the substance should be consecrated with mantras, for otherwise there would be a lack of effort.
Without the perfuming of substances, the mantra becomes mere memory;
those great fools who merely remember it encounter suffering at every step.
There is no drinking without mantra, nor should one contemplate the mantra without drinking. How could the substance be perfected? By what means would there be worship?
Beholding, touching, and sprinkling with water according to reality bestow purity upon substances;
likewise, the Yonimudrā and that called Mṛtā should be observed by those whose domain is mantra.
Then, having performed the lineage of gurus (gurukrama) and recollecting the feet of the guru,
my teachers must make me a single vessel, indeed a worthy recipient.
The foolish ones [practice] the rapid pacification through the command of the five jewels and the nectar;
likewise, they [recite] the Gāyatrī with liquor, as well as Ānandabhairava.
The goddess Ānandabhairavī releases the curse of semen;
one should recite each [mantra] eight times and then perform the libation.
Substance, flesh, the sacrificial vessel, the consort, and the honeyed person—O Goddess, may bliss arise from these; I bow to that which is of a single form.
The Goddess said:
Through the non-dual practice of the five offerings without substitution for the Goddess, one moves within the center of the Bhairavī-cakra; everything becomes pure, like nectar.
All the birds there subsisted on leaves; there was no change whatsoever, whether they had three bowls, five bowls, or even seven bowls.
As long as nothing has been given to us, it is declared that drinking [of wine] occurs;
the substance would be unrefined, and sexual intercourse would be by force.
O Goddess, by sprinkling both [of these], one goes to hell;
O Goddess, this is the definitive conclusion of the scripture regarding the collection of the Command.
Drinking from a single vessel constitutes the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such grave offenses;
one should drink substances left over by Śaktis, and chew what is left over by Vīras.
Likewise, one should not consume the remnants of a hero, nor forbidden substances, nor the remnants of Śakti, nor that which has been chewed;
one must not do so within the circle (cakra), otherwise there will be a fall.
O Goddess, when a man seeks union with a woman during the period of *nandā* or *vasā*, sexual intercourse should be performed there; no hesitation should be made in this matter.
3b) A second sacrifice should be performed with that same substance, which bestows liberation;
in some cases one should practice drinking, in some cases meditation, and in some cases chewing.
Drinking without chewing merely increases poison;
when there is chewing, that very drinking is proclaimed to be nectar.
The Goddess said:
By whom was this vessel, consisting of eight types of substances, fashioned?
O Virūpākṣa, what is the state of Śakti, and what is the supreme Śakti like?
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain how many substances there are here:
that made from molasses (gauḍī), the nourishing one (pauṣṭī), as well as that made from honey (mādhvī), from dates (khārjurī), and from coconut (nārikelajā).
Wine made from palm-juice and rice, and grape-wine—these are the eight kinds of liquor.
That produced from molasses is called *gauḍī*, and that produced from flour is called *paiṣṭī*.
O Goddess, Mādhvī is produced from Madhuka flowers, while Chāndrī arises from all types of rice grains;
Gauḍī is to be accepted by those who know the enjoyment [of wine], whereas Mādhvī bestows liberation.
The liquor made from flour (*paiṣṭī*) brings about all accomplishments; that made from dates (*kharjurī*) destroys enemies;
that produced from palmyra palm (*tālaja*) is said to be for paralyzing; and coconut liquor (*nārikela*) is for enchanting.
Attraction and expulsion are said [to be achieved] by means of wine; the method for killing is prescribed as follows:
grapes and royal power are to be taken [as results], while other [results] are obtained in the case of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
4a) O Dear One, [the meat] of elephants, horses, humans, cows, goats, boars, buffaloes,
and rhinoceroses constitutes the great eightfold group of meats (māṃsāṣṭaka).
The washerwoman, the fisherwoman, the outcaste woman, the Vala and Aṅganā,
the cowherd’s wife, and the courtesan— these are the powers (śaktis) born from the essence of flowers.

One who has deficient or extra limbs, improper conduct, a harsh nature, or who demands payment for her services, and who is devoid of compassion and devotion— such a woman is to be avoided during the ritual of the Parvan.
She who has beautiful teeth, is joyful, capable, well-formed, and sprinkled with power—
she who follows the family dharma should be worshipped with great effort.
Substances that have been kept for a long time, substances devoid of fragrance,
those that are remnants of a meal, those that are foul-smelling, and those from inferior sacred sites should be avoided.
The flesh of the daughter’s beloved should never be taken by the initiates;
rather, all those who have been initiated are to be gathered together in a single vessel for the consumption.
The Goddess said:

When should worship be performed? What is the power of sacred fords (tīrtha) in this world? What should be accepted through the influence of passion (mada)? And what occurs in the presence of power and childhood?
What is the fruit of daily worship, or what occurs when Śiva is worshipped?
For one who is incapable, having gratified a *paśu*, the daily worship becomes accomplished through *jayā*.
Then what indeed should be done? By whom was the vessel fashioned?
By whom should the support be made? In this matter, you ought to concern yourself with liberation.
The illustrious Lord said:
Daily worship should be performed, as well as that on the five festival days (parvan) whenever they occur;
the threefold method of worship is to be carried out for one month.
On the eighth, the ninth, and the fourteenth,
as well as on the eleventh, one should likewise worship with the pārvaṇa rite, O Maheśvarī, the Great Goddess of all the gods.
Worship performed constantly is the highest; worship on the five festival days (parvan) is middling;
worship once a month is the lowest; and beyond a month, one becomes a beast.
One who has fallen away from all dharmas should practice the Kaula dharma;
one who has fallen away from the Kaula dharma shall go to the Raurava hell.
Milk, curd, ghee, molasses, oil, and substances derived from sulfur;
likewise, fresh rainwater and coconut water.
O beautiful one, it is taught that these eight substances are absent when the primary substance is absent;
namely, the fish-tail ornament, the cock, and the partridge.
O beloved, in the absence of the eight meats, one should always perform worship with oil-cake, boiled meat, salt, and ginger, O Gṛṣṭini.
O Queen of the Gods, in the absence of [external] power, one should worship the power of one's own Self.
And drinking is said to be of three kinds, in the sequence of the Divine (daiva), the Heroic (vīra), and the Fettered (paśu).
5a) The wise one should perform the drinking of wine with the god and goddess, along with the three [substances] of *śakti* and meat,
and the five *makāras*, in a secluded place there.
Having practiced the five [substances] beginning with "M"— namely, human flesh (mahāmāṃsa), fish (matsya), mudrā, sexual union (maithuna), and liquor (madya)— rebirth no longer exists.

Having sat upon the ground of the garden in silence and placed the triangle on his head, he drank that; indeed, this is known as the "hero’s drink" (vīrapāna), which is like nectar brought from the dead.
One who is devoid of mantras and yantras, devoted to the way of the Paśus, and intent on drinking liquor;
and [those possessing] gold, silver, pearls, coral, and likewise gold.
Crystal, coconut-seed, coral, and excellent pearl are [auspicious];
gold grants all desires, and silver bestows all prosperity.
Crystal grants subjugation to men; the coconut shell bestows the eight siddhis; glass is the means for malevolent rites (abhicāra); and coral is used for acts of attraction (ākarṣaṇa).
A pearl bestows liberation upon men, while a human skull grants the perfection of mantras;
likewise, [vessels made of] copper, bell-metal, iron, clay, or wood [are effective].
One should avoid a vessel made of the three metals, bone, or horn;
likewise, a vessel for the support [of the ritual] is said to be made of the three metals or of such materials.
"Excluding copper and bell-metal, everything else is known as the vessel for the *ojas*.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth [chapter] in the *Śrīsāmabhujavallī*, the *Kaurasārasaṃgraha*, within the dialogue between the God and the Goddess.
Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"Non-violence is the supreme dharma," so it was known by the sages of old;
yet what you have said, O Lord, is certainly contrary to that.
How could one perform the most terrible injury to living beings with great joy?
O Lord, how should one perform worship within the Śāmbhava state, which is free from doubt?
The illustrious Lord said:
There is no doubt that Śiva and Śakti are superimposed as both distinct and non-distinct;
when the Goddess is saluted, worship consists in the performance of actions free from desire.
There is no sin equal to the killing of a human being, nor is there one like the drinking of liquor;
likewise, there is no other [sin] as grave as approaching another's wife when it is seen to have been committed.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin do not afflict the Kaulikas at all;
just as drops of water do not cling to the petals of a lotus.
Even if one were to kill a Brahmin, if they both smile,
that vessel which was obtained at the end will certainly be emptied by their drinking from it.
If one does not obtain flesh situated in the center of the Bhairavī-cakra, for that purpose one may kill a cow and a Brahmin; no fault is found.
For through right conduct one attains prosperity, and by conduct the subjects become smiling;
even the gods are well-pleased with the bond of right conduct.
Good conduct must always be abandoned by sages who have extracted [the essence] from the world.
Whether it be a man devoid of proper conduct, a Kaulika, or even a mere beast, the Goddesses serve him in three ways; what fruit, then, can there be from his mantra?
The Kaulas should avoid these five: performing penance, throwing oneself from a cliff, renunciation, observing vows, and going on pilgrimages to sacred sites.
Whatever sin afflicts a man, it is not removed by a penance performed for that purpose;
however, falling from a cliff or entering the fire is the destroyer of even the most heinous crimes (mahāpātaka).
The supreme mistress of Maheśvara, residing in the water, is the bestowal of the fruit of all desires;
the son of noble family who abides [in her] attains the fruit of all vows.
By even a single drop of Vāruṇī, one obtains the merit of ten million sacred fords;
it is declared to be the expiation for all sins whatsoever.
For those who are detached from family duties, there is neither sight nor hearing of anything anywhere;
the practitioner of mantra should always worship her as a mother would her own son.
If someone situated in the center of the Śrīcakra performs the rite for Bhairava, then everyone must eat his leftovers; it is not prescribed by scripture that they should eat otherwise.
If a person should cause a sūtra to be altered, that very person becomes purified;
even if a person’s entire body were afflicted with leprosy at some point.
One should feed the remnants of the Śrīcakra to the disciple; he shall become pure.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Kuvera, and Indra—all these [reside] in the turning of the Śrīcakra.
One should indeed worship the human being in this way; she will attain [success], of this there is no doubt.
What more need be said? That man has become one with Brahman who has reached the Kaulika path; what further [attainment] can there be for a man through the door of Brahmā?
The Vaiśya’s power through the solar extraction (bhānukarṣa) for the purpose of subduing those in foreign lands is truly immense;
how could the gods possibly be equal to him?
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the *Kulasārasaṃgraha*, the illustrious *Somabhujangalī*.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Tripurā.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the manual of the conduct of the samaya;
by knowing which, O Great Goddess, the practitioner shall attain accomplishment.
The Lord said:
One should not transgress the command of the guru, nor speak back to him;
whether by night or by day, one should obey his command like a servant.
The consciousness of liberation at the end of the transition to another state is eternally pervaded by the venerable Guru; therefore, one should proceed according to his instruction.
One should never show indifference toward tasks, whether they have been explicitly stated or left unsaid;
one should follow behind the teacher as he walks and must not step over his shadow.
Disregarding the words of the guru and turning one's back on the feet [of the teacher],
whether what is heard be beneficial or harmful, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
Thus, a wise person should never treat such a teacher with contempt.
O Goddess, he of deluded intellect who violates the command of the Guru goes to a terrible hell and shall attain the state of a Piśāca.
One must never cause anyone to commit the violation of an order, nor the censuring of the guru, nor the instigation [of others against him],
nor any act of treachery toward the guru.
Desire for the property of a guru, as well as sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru—
his state of being a sinner is fixed, and he shall not be released by means of penance.
Having uttered "huṃ" and "huṃ," and having quickly defeated [his opponent] in debate,
he shall become a brahmarākṣasa in a lonely place in the forest.
Upon seeing the sandals, seat, garment, bed, or ornaments of the guru, one should bow and not use them for one's own enjoyment.
He on the tip of whose tongue the mantra of the Śrīpādukā always resides shall effortlessly attain virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
In great disease, in great calamity, in great hardship, in great fear,
in great misfortune, and in great sin— may the Guru’s sandals protect me!
I bow to the pair of feet of the Guru, whose form is existence-consciousness-bliss;
this supreme union of Śiva and Śakti is distinguished by the colors white and red.
7b) In whichever direction the lotus feet of Śrīnātha shine,
one should pay homage to that direction with body, mind, and speech.
A disciple residing in the same village should prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day;
a disciple residing in a distant land should prostrate to the guru once every month.
O Dear One, the mantra that is superior to all knowledge, scriptures, and tantras must certainly be obtained in its entirety from the mouth of every guru; it is not otherwise.
O beloved, sitting on the same seat as one's teacher is forbidden in a deceptive place, on a wooden beam, in a palace, in a narrow passage, on a long piece of wood, or on the surface of a stone.
Whatever object is beneficial to oneself, one should never deceive that substance;
[this applies to] the *pādukā* mantra of the venerable Guru and the *pādukā* of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
O Goddess, speak this to your disciples, but do not speak it to just anyone;
by offering libations and gifts to the Guru, I am pleased, O lady of excellent vows.
O lady of excellent vows, I am pleased with him who is devoted solely to the service of the guru;
for whatever he does, directed toward the guru, is performed with devotion according to his intention.

He who, devoid of devotion to the Guru, might give even his entire wealth to another out of poverty, though that other person has performed great service for him with only a little; [such a gift is fruitless].
One incurs affliction through pride; indeed, devotion alone is the cause [of liberation].
One should never proclaim the faults of the guru’s wife, children, or kinsmen.
One should consume the substance offered for sprinkling, but one should not give it away nor cast it aside;
this applies even to a maiden, a girl, a hero, a yoginī, or a kaulika.
8a) A woman, even if she belongs to another caste or class, must never be treated with contempt;
nor should one strike her, even if she has committed a grave offense, just as one would not pluck a flower from a tree.
One should not proclaim the faults of the city [of the body] nor the divine qualities.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Devotion to the Guru," in the *Śrīkulācāranirṇaya*.
O Dear One, one should neither recite nor meditate without the dwelling of the substance;
those great fools who perform worship in such a manner encounter suffering at every step.
The Goddess said:
Without the substance there is no mantra, and without the mantra there is no finger;
since they are mutually dependent, how can the worship be performed?
Through looking, smelling, and meditating, various substances are purified;
having drunk that, the recollection and worship of all mantras become beneficial.
One should perform the supreme consecration of the five substances with the mantra;
O Goddess of the Gods, with that which has been purified, one should satisfy the deity of the Kula.
Inspection, sprinkling, meditation, and the purification of mantras, mudrās, and so forth—such substances become fit for touch; otherwise, they would be fruitless.
Always endowed with devotion and intent upon the propitiation of the mantra,
one should offer the kula-substance together with the oral instruction of the mantra.
He should perform the satiation of the family substance with the left hand using fingernails;
he attains identity with the deity— this is the truth, O Maheśvarī.
The thumb is considered the goddess Bhairavī, and the middle finger is regarded as Caṇḍikā.
One should satisfy the family deity by joining the middle finger with the thumb;
and for rites pertaining to dharma, one should satisfy [the deities] with the thumb and the ring finger.
One should perform the libation using the union of the index finger and the thumb in rites of sorcery;
using the union of the little finger and the thumb in rites of immobilization and the subjugation of spirits.
If one performs the libation otherwise, it shall be fruitless;
O Kuleśvarī, as long as one does not offer to Vaṭuka, so long [the rite] is not at all [complete].
When the offering is first given to Sundarī, the worship becomes threefold. May all the Mothers, along with the Rudras and the host of deities, be satisfied.
One should offer the bali to Vaṭuka in the south, the bali to the Yoginīs in the north,
the bali to the Bhūtas in the east, and to the guardians of the site in the west.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess, the Queen of the Queens of Kings, in the center;
then, one should offer the bali-oblation to Vaṭuka using the thumb and ring finger.
One should offer the bali to the Yoginīs using the joined little finger and thumb;
the bali for Kṣetrapāla is considered to be offered with the thumb and index finger.
O beloved, it is taught that with all the fingers one offers the *bhūtabali*;
likewise, with the thumb and the middle finger, one offers to the Lord of the Kings of Kings.
One should offer the family substances for the sake of the deity according to the scriptures;
by my grace, one obtains everything desired—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Kulācāranirṇaya* composed by Śiva.
9a) For men performing my rites, should there be an omission of the ritual action,
they perform it according to the prescriptions of their family tradition (*kulācāra*).
O beloved, thirty crores of great sages have declared that worship performed without the mandala is fruitless for one who desires the highest goal.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship that very [energy] according to the prescribed rite—
she who stands pervading the entire universe in the form of an unbroken circle.
By him the three worlds are adorned; Sadāśiva is indeed the maṇḍala.
Oḍiyāna is square, while Kāmarūpa is circular.
Jālandhara is the half-moon, and Pūrṇagiri is copper;
the support (ādhāra) is said to be of three kinds, consisting of six parts or four parts.
Alternatively, one should make it circular, beautiful and captivating,
fashioned from gold, silver, stone, tortoise-shell, conch, or clay.
A wise person should prepare a vessel made of coconut, conch, or that which originates from pearl-oyster shells, or one produced from a sacred tree.
One should not have vessels made of copper, bell-metal, or other metals;
rather, [the offering] should consist of leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, bark, or products derived from grain.
The juice-tree, the vine-palm, and the substance are recorded as being of ten kinds:
*pāla*, *drākṣā*, *mādhūka*, *khārjūra*, *tāla*, and *aikṣava*.
Mādhūka āsava, sidhu, maireya, and that produced from coconut—
these eleven types of liquor bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And the twelfth substance for liquor is the most excellent of all.
[One may offer] liquor produced from milk-trees, that arising from the bark of the *māhya* tree,
that produced from the juice of honey-flowers, or that produced from rice-husks.
The offering of *gauḍī* bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*) and grants enjoyment; *mādhvī* is said to grant liberation (*mukti*); and *drākṣī* grants sovereignty.

The palm-born [wine] is said to paralyze; the date-palm wine destroys enemies; that produced from coconuts bestows prosperity; and drinking [the wine] made from grapes is always considered to grant happiness.
Mādhvī is said to bestow knowledge, while sāriṣṭā removes disease.
Flesh is said to be of three kinds: that of aquatic, aerial, and terrestrial creatures.
O Goddess, the eight great meats— including the flesh of the elephant, the horse, the human, the boar, and the deer— bring delight to the deities.
That which is offered into another's vessel by means of nails that are broken, discolored, foul-smelling, or devoid of fragrance shall be fruitless.
O Maheśānī, with the *ariṣṭa* substances and the *vasārīya* materials which are like nectar,
one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*), which bestows the fruits of all desires.
Due to the absence of materials such as meat and other offerings, one might constantly neglect the obligatory rite;
if there is such a lapse through negligence, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
Buttermilk, milk, jaggery, honey, curd, ghee, sesame, sugar, bamboo shoots, and lotus stalks— these are recorded as the ten kinds of substances.
Salt, ginger, oil-cake, wheat, and the five kinds of meat.
And Guñjana, O Maheśānī; these are remembered as the ten kinds of meat.
Among those mentioned, one may use whichever substance is available according to the circumstances.
From the eight fragrances they arise; one should satisfy them with these juices.
The conch, the right hand, and the vessels for the offerings are indeed used in their proper sequence.
But the Vāmācārya, having established Dakṣa and the others, should grind [the substance] with flour;
and he who is capable may consume the Kula-substance even without it being formally offered.
The deity incurs a curse and the worship becomes fruitless;
[one should therefore receive initiation] according to one's own capacity or the capacity of the Guru, having been initiated from the mouth of the Guru.
The experts in the scriptures know that one should drink [the water] after having caused it to be sung over by these substances:
a courtesan, a female vintner, a fisherwoman, and likewise a washerwoman.
Tantukārī, Kāmārī, Mātaṅgī, and likewise Undhasī—
this is declared to be the eightfold family (kulāṣṭaka), and it is called the eightfold auspicious ones (maṅgalāṣṭaka).
Whether she be a maiden, one established in a vow, or even one who bears the yoga-mudrā—
she who is prescribed at the time of worship is called the "innate" (sahajā) libation by the wise.
In the state of the consort (sadyaṅganā), worship proceeds through the four castes day by day;
she is beautiful, youthful, peaceful, of noble lineage, joyful, and pure.
Complete in her limbs, endowed with devotion, initiated according to the Kula scripture,
captivating, and of virtuous conduct— such is this Śakti, possessed of auspicious marks.
She is wicked, fierce, harsh, cruel, envious, and a defiler of her family;
she is ill-behaved, dependent on others, devoid of truth, and full of lustful desire.

One who is asleep, one who is distracted, one of dull intellect, one with missing limbs, one afflicted by disease, one of evil appearance, or one associated with an enemy— such a woman is to be avoided in the ritual union with the messenger (dūtī).
Thus ends the third chapter in the Śrīkulācāra as spoken by Śiva.

Now, the primary rule for the full-moon festival (pārvaṇa) of the Goddess Tripurā, which has not yet been discussed, is written here: during a vyatīpāta yoga, at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), during lunar or solar eclipses,
on the day when the Deśika, the Ācārya, and the Yoginīs have all come together.
For practitioners, the offerings of grain-husks and oblations are wasted;
otherwise, the rays of the Guru-Indra turn away in disfavor.
One should employ the final sequence for Phalguvalī when she is detached;
otherwise, the Yoginīs become angry with him and dry up his essence and flesh.
Thus ends the procedure for the ritual offerings to the Goddess Tripurā according to the inner Kaulika doctrine.
Having practiced the five [elements] beginning with *m*— namely, liquor (*madya*), meat (*māṃsa*), fish (*matsya*), parched grain (*mudrā*), and sexual union (*maithuna*)— rebirth no longer exists.
The Goddess said:
When the circle of Gopinis is active, all castes become twice-born;
when the circle of Yoginis has ceased, all castes remain distinct.
The single wheel and the separate bowl were established according to the order of seniority.
The initiate, the practitioner, the son, the teacher, and likewise the yoginī—
those who belong to the noble family (kulīna) of the single wheel are all worthy vessels of the lineage.
One should eat together with these people, along with the food; of this there is no doubt.
One should not use a single vessel, nor should one use separate vessels.
Having obtained the substance for the practice, one should remain focused with a single thought and concentrated;
no hesitation should be made here, for once it is performed, death will occur.
By what state of mind was this devotion and self-restraint performed?
Through that, liberation shall be his; he shall become like the moon, the Guru.
One attains the supreme state, which is difficult even for the gods to reach;
indeed, by knowing this Kaulika conduct, one shall obtain perfection.
When a gathering has arrived, or during an initiation ceremony, or on a festival day, one may bring [offerings] for the sake of worship;
but never for one's own sake alone.
O Goddess of gods, one who performs the auspicious Pārvaṇa rite endowed with self-control obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices as well as the merit of giving hundreds of loads of gold.
But by giving to the Kaulikas even a mere drop [of wine] through union with a woman,
one obtains the merit of the earth filled with gold and the gift of ten million maidens.
That fruit and the bestowal of power [occur] in the Kaulika sacrificial hall;
with an abundance of many flowers, he established ten million *liṅgas*.
O Goddess, one obtains that fruit; the Yoginī shall become a bestower of boons.
Obstacles will certainly not arise, and success shall be attained without hindrance;
all the Mothers, along with their hosts and Vināyakas, will be satisfied.
The hosts of gods, the sages of Brahmā’s gate, and the auspicious ones are satisfied; as are the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those who are lower still.
Those who, driven by greed, engage in [the practice] while devoid of ritual action, lacking knowledge, and bereft of power and wisdom, drink the wine of this [world].
In this regard, austerity must be performed, as well as falling [into the mandala] again and again;
likewise, the Guru, the deity, the scripture, the mandala, and the Krama-yoginī.
In the ritual application, one should perform the invocation; by touching [the image], one shall become a possessor of siddhi.
The sins committed throughout seven lifetimes, as well as those incurred in the Raurava hell, [shall be destroyed].
By the mere sight of the substance, one becomes sinless in an instant;
likewise in the science of medicine, in the Veda, and especially in the case of a devotee.
One should act immediately upon merely seeing [the object]; otherwise, the loss of accomplishment occurs.
One should feel neither disgust nor doubt if one desires long life.
One who is not a worthy recipient should not accept [an offering]; if he enters the womb [of a woman] after being consecrated, O Goddess, by accepting him, one incurs a curse upon one's own head.
That which is circular in the center of the wheel is auspicious for one's own day;
it is auspicious by day, and at dawn it should be declared as "tanu"— such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
No food whatsoever exists, nor does even water exist.
Having abandoned the wives of the guru and heroes, as well as all other beautiful women,
those who enter the Great Goddess and those who enter the Yoginī—
And their suppression, O Goddess, occurs by examining the primary seat;
all those practitioners who revile [the teaching] shall perish, for they are detractors.
May the state of Śāmbhavī be attained and may the Guru always be gracious. That which is known as the rule for the day is said to be the "day" even at night.
Having discerned the distinction by means of light, one should perform worship at night;
those who speak ill of or disparage the Kaulikas should not be described.
If the meaning of that which consists of the bliss of the glorious Jñānin were concealed,
then the Kaulikas would desire the state of a bound soul (paśu).
The taste of the dharma, its decline, and that Yoginī herself shall incur sin;
one should abandon drinking for the sake of the Guru, or likewise even for the sake of the Deity.
Then, having placed the hand of the Goddess upon his head, that man, together with his mother and fathers,
having entered the path of his lineage, exerted himself with great strength.
O Goddess, one who has committed a great sin (mahāpātakin) should not be made to perform the Prayāsa penance; however, she may be appointed through another method for the sake of protecting Dharma.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on the conduct of the *samaya* in the *Kramasūtra*, within the *Kaulikavidāna* of the *Kutrikātantra*, concerning the descent into the sacred seats (*pīṭha*).
12b) He who practices without knowing the measure for taking life, as well as the throat and the characteristics [of the channels], will fall from calamity to calamity.
Today, [the deity] possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, having ascended from the root-triangle (mūlatrikoṇa), resides in the fire of the awakened Kuṇḍalinī-śakti;
[therein is] the Kula-substance together with the Mātṛkās.
The *caruka* is said to bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*), and the lamp bestows knowledge;
through drinking, the highest attainment is reached—this triad is supreme in the *Kaula* tradition.

One should contemplate with the intellect the oneness of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra until the state of intense spiritual exhilaration (ullāsa) is reached; through such instructions, one should drink the honey of nectar.
Drinking accompanied by chewing is proclaimed to be nectar;
drinking without chewing is merely an increase of poison.
Drink is said to be of three kinds, in the sequence of divine, heroic, and animal. Divine drink is [offered] before the Goddess; heroic drink is for one who dwells in solitude.

Drinking liquor according to one's own will is known as "animal-like drinking" (paśupāna); furthermore, drinking liquor devoid of ritual injunctions and mantras is likewise considered animal-like drinking.
O beloved, enjoyment and liberation, as well as hell which is the fruit thereof,
exist only so long as the vision does not move and so long as the mind does not move.
One should perform drinking only to that extent; beyond this is the "drinking of the beast.
For one whose limbs are deficient due to lacking the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), drinking leads to extreme misfortune.
For those who are endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), drinking is highly recommended;
having drunk, and having drunk again, and having drunk once more, he falls to the ground.
Having risen and drunk again, rebirth is no longer found.
The vessel is Brahmā, the nectar is Viṣṇu, the bubbles are the deities Rudra.
Āmoda is said to be the crest-ornament; may Sadāśiva be ever blissful.
The power of will (icchā-śakti) resides in the wine, and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in its flavor.
Therefore, O beloved, one should always remain in that eternal bliss which arises from ritual action;
for the substance is Śakti, Śiva is the meat, and Bhairava himself is its consumer.
The supreme power, whose seat is identical to that [of the self], is called bliss and liberation;
bliss is the form of Brahman, and it is established within the body.
Therefore, that manifesting substance is drunk by the yogis;
singers sing it to the end, and yogis meditate upon it through mantras.
Those intoxicated by lust take their pleasure; the intoxicated provoke anger.
[This is done] for the purpose of recollecting mantras and so forth, as a cause for stabilizing the mind.
One should consume meat that has been killed for the sake of removing fear and affliction,
for the benefit of all the gods, and for the stabilization of the knowledge of Brahman.
They never consume honey or meat out of greed;
[they offer] thousands of jars of ghee and hundreds of jars of milk.
By means of the bee, through a mere drop, they deserve the sixteenth digit;
it has flowed down, melted by the union of the moon, sun, and fire.
With that divine nectar of immortality, one should satisfy the supreme Guru,
either through the Kula scriptures of the illustrious Guru or by means of the Kula of perfect knowledge.
O beloved, family property is maintained through prohibition and not otherwise.
The gurus [attain] the supreme space characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
O beloved, the realization of the kula-substance arises [from them], and not otherwise.

O beloved, by drinking the nectar of aesthetic flavor (rasāmṛta) through the mind, speech, and body directed toward the innermost Self within the heart, [liberation] arises; it does not happen otherwise.
One should reveal the perfected substances to the noble ones among the Kaulikas.
O Pārvatī, when the nectar is purified by the consecration of mantra and drunk,
the state of the deity arises, which destroys even the greatest of sins.
Well-prepared, it removes the disease of liquor, suffering, and poverty; if unprepared, it becomes a source of affliction, strife, and illness, yet even then it destroys misery.
One should satisfy this substance of the eight Bhairavas with pure substances;
the sin of killing a Brahmin and the sin of killing an embryo are destroyed—of this there is no doubt.
A drop of wine destroys the sins committed over seven lifetimes;
yet even a hero, having drunk it during the ritual of animal sacrifice, goes to hell.
By violating the distinction between the male organ and the female organ, one goes to the Raurava hell;
likewise for drinking unprepared substances or engaging in sexual intercourse by force.
Having killed an animal with one's own hand, one shall go to the Raurava hell;
one should employ [the ritual] even if it lacks libations, lacks fire-offerings, lacks power, or lacks strength.
14a) And the libation performed devoid of the second [element] would be fruitless;
likewise for one who, without knowing the family tradition (kulācāra), touches the sandals of the Guru.
In whatever ritual manual this beast among yoginīs might engage,
there is neither wine without the substance, nor is there a woman without the substance.
Without that second [officiant], one would go to the Raurava hell;
without the *jājñaka* mantra, and without the mantra, one who performs a sacrifice [falls].
Never shall there be attainment of the fruit, nor would the sacrifice be fruitless;
one should never reveal oneself through another's body.
One may become a sacrificial animal through the measure of one's lack of steadfastness regarding place and time;
therefore, do not undertake pilgrimages, nor perform sacrifices, nor even [other rites].
For he who is always devoted to fasting and vows should bow to everything with the thought that it is his guru, and likewise prostrate before the deities.
He should be born into a noble family and avoid speaking in opposition;
he should never cause those who are devoid of the power of mantra to perform prostrations.
Those who know the path of the Vedas recognize that the word, the sentence, and the authoritative scripture are the means of knowledge;
one should never cause those devoid of the traditional family instructions to perform prostration.
O beloved, one should cause those who are attached to their family traditions, who are hostile, who follow evil conduct, and who are excessively arrogant or negligent, to perform prostrations.
Fish, meat, and a jar of liquor shall bring success to the mantras;
so too shall mangoes, leafy vegetables, and playful young maidens.
Having seen a solitary tree, a cremation ground, those places of worship,
and women with faces like the autumn moon, I pay homage with devotion.
One should never perform worship without the śrīpātra vessel;
for if one performs it otherwise, the worship shall become fruitless.
If a disciple who has been initiated and possesses the mantra has gone to heaven while still in the city [of the body],
the consecration for the primordial yoga (*prādiyogābhiṣecana*) must not take place until there is only one remaining lineage member.
Even a youth who was initiated first and belongs to the elder brother's lineage shall be the elder;
even one who is old and initiated later shall be the younger—of this there is no doubt.

Whether a twice-born man is initiated later while another born of a lower caste was initiated earlier, that twice-born man is the younger and the other is the elder; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
The meat of a guru, of a guru’s daughters, or of a disciple— these should not be consumed by one another,
nor should one worship them while they are present, just as one would not do so in the presence of a city.
O Great Goddess, one who shows miserliness toward a son, a wife, all women,
or for the sake of a guru, shall go to the Raurava hell.

One should not perform worship, offerings, and so forth toward the group of gurus or the group of elders; one should not carry out such practice, but rather cause it to be performed by those who are auspicious.
15a) The elder [initiate] is one who has been consecrated by mantras and is exempt from the water-consecration (abhiṣeka) and other rites;
the younger [initiate] should perform the sequential worship (kramapūjā) in whichever direction is complete.
The forehead, face, round eyes, ears, nose, cheeks, lips, teeth, lower body, and the joints and graspings of the arms; |||
Having first performed [the rites] on the two sides, the back, the navel, the belly, the region of the heart,
and the part of the hump, one should likewise perform them on the hands and feet.
O Pārvatī, having offered all of that in due order to the deities of the belly, ending with the final one among the Mātṛkās, one should eat the remainder.
The *sthambhana* [mudrā] is square, as are the *matsya*, *gomukha*, *yoni*, and the renowned *surabhi*; these five mudrās are saluted with reverence.
Whether it be the guru, the guru’s wife, or the son,
or the elder sister who performs the worship in the middle, one should immediately abandon the worship of the disciple.
"A disciple should worship according to the command; such is the conclusion of the scripture.
This applies to the Guru's elder wife as well as to the Mistress of the Bakula grove."
Without sitting down, there is no determination of the substance according to the treatise;
the substance placed in one's own vessel is for the sake of salutation to Bhairava.
That man would suffer the loss of his spiritual accomplishment and encounter calamities at every step;
however, through the divine drink, supreme bliss arises.
15b) Then,
having stolen that which belongs to oneself or one's wife, one shall go to the Raurava hell;
likewise for stealing a vessel of offerings given by another, or the sandals, or the root mantra.
It must be taken within the center of the *cakra*; otherwise, a fall [from grace] will occur.
One should not use a single vessel unless the Mistress of the Kula is present in person.
The mantras turn away and misfortunes arise at every step [for one who consumes] fish,
meat, as well as liquor, [forbidden] hand-gestures, and sexual intercourse.
O fair-faced one, one should practice devotion to the Guru for the sake of satisfaction;
this mudrā destroys poverty and takes on a form that removes the mine of suffering.
It pacifies the disease of leprosy; therefore, one should always worship this mudrā with those who are uninitiated, of improper conduct, and devoid of undesirable qualities.
"That animal must indeed be sacrificed; such is the firm conclusion of the scriptures.
One who observes the rules must certainly perform the rite with the substance; he attains that [result]."
One should not entrust one's wealth to other men who are uncorrupted but reside in another country, except through a formal agreement.
One who desires the divine power should never, even for a moment, allow others to take away one's seat, bedding, food, clothing, or ornaments.

O Goddess, one who has not been initiated should perform the Śrīcakra for the sake of purification through association with the virtuous, even if he engages in the consumption of food and drink [with such persons].
One should not eat while women, one's teacher, or an elder are asleep; nor should one eat without being invited, nor should one cut off a connection by not going when invited.
A Yoginī who is utterly deluded regarding the Śrīcakra shall incur a curse;
at the end of her meal is the drinking of poison, and at the end of her drink is food that is poison.
Having eaten and drunk, one should offer the family property.
One incurs the curse of the deities and shall go to the Raurava hell;
at the end of a meal, drink is poison, and at the end of drinking, food is poison.
One should understand that to be nectar; such is the meaning. And if that very [substance] is broken within the wheel, or falls into a jar, or into a vessel—
If the lamp is extinguished or the ritual implements are lost, one should again construct the Śrīcakra;
furthermore, that person of deluded intellect who holds the vessel or places it down [is at fault].
The yoginī incurs a curse and meets with calamities at every step if she fails,
through negligence, to perform the worship and communal feast (goṣṭha) for those who effect worldly benefits.
His worship shall be fruitless, and that Yoginī shall incur a curse;
moreover, one who is devoid of the fundamental initiation (mūladīkṣā) shall always be excluded from worship.
Having incurred the curse of the Guru, one shall receive the curse of the Yoginīs;
one should drink the substance with only one hand, and likewise, it should be offered without the mudrā.
O Lord of the Night, one should worship the family deity on a single seat in the terrible Sarvasainnanaraka hell for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
One should also understand the *sapusta* and perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*);
likewise, the body (*gātra*), the canopy (*vitāna*), and the favor and form of the *kaula*.
That which is a downfall in the world is not a production of divinity in one's lineage; for that which is supreme in the world may be base, and likewise, what is valorous may be most excellent.
16b) Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the yoga of mantra according to the prescribed rule;
the practitioner, being afflicted, should perform worship with a focused mind.
In a forest region or a village where others do not dwell, both types of reciters are born;
one should remember that a seat has been offered in that place, O Jayanta, and not from a mandala.
Thus ends the chapter in the *Śrīkulācāranirṇaya*.
The means for the complete attainment of the eightfold reality for a living being is now declared;
indeed, the supreme attainment is prescribed in every way for both the knowers and the performers of action.
Action merges into knowledge, and through knowledge, one attains the state of Śiva;
liberation consists precisely in oneness with Śiva, therefore one should perform all actions.
If one’s teacher has attained universal pervasion (*paravyāpti*), whether he be the eldest,
the youngest, or even oneself, [the disciple] becomes a teacher by virtue of having attained that state.
Or else, having offered it by means of oneself through some [means], one should cause the attainment of the fruit;
for that which arises from intense knowledge and action is immediate in Śiva, whereas the other is slow.
Having known his own death, he should, before that, on the seventh day,
or the fifth, or the third, or the first, according to his capacity, [perform the rites].
O Goddess, beginning from that day, every day at the feet of your image,
on the day prior to the anniversary of my death, I shall perform worship along with groups of kinsmen and officiating priests.
And having worshipped with all ritual offerings the supreme Guru seated in their midst, who was resplendent, along with the yoginīs and those who offer ritual substances;
17a) Having prostrated, O Lord, forgive me here, who have acted contrary to your will;
whatever evil deed has been committed by me, be gracious and make it virtuous.
Having thus informed the Guru, the disciple [should offer] his own three births and deaths,
as well as his servants, children, wife, and so forth, along with his body and mind.
Having informed the Guru, "Please accept all of this," one should offer it to him;
for the Guru is pervaded by the Supreme, and within this [offering] lies the venerable *pādukā* of the Guru.
Having established [the deity] upon a pure seat and worshipped it, one should indeed present the offering.
O Lord, in the event of inability to perform the worship due to illness or other causes, it may be done with lotuses.
One should have the worship of the Guru performed by those who are senior, junior, or even predecessors;
for upon his death, there is no other Guru, owing to the absence of both the existent and the non-existent.
Then, one should divide all the wealth acquired therein into four parts;
having given two shares to [one's own] wives, one should likewise give the other two to other women.

Two shares are allotted for the daughter's son, two shares each for the two [categories of] officiating priests, one share for the teacher, and one share for the members of the assembly; and in the absence of the teacher, [the shares go] to the teacher’s family.
Having bestowed the blessing upon him here, and afterwards having washed [the vessel] and adorned it with flowers and other offerings,
one should bathe the [deity] brought from the cremation ground and install it there.
One should install [the deity] within his body by means of the sequence of withdrawal;
having taken [the essence] with the *sahīra* mudrā, he becomes the vehicle of that deity.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own body, ending with the fifty [phonemes] in the all-devouring Śāntā;
having meditated upon the venerable Bhairava according to the *tantra* and bowed to the two pairs of the Self and the Consort.
Salutation to the one who consumes obstacles as his wealth, whose speech is pure like the rising sun,
the great fire, the great light, and the sole oblation for the universe.
Having thus recited the mantra, one should offer the oblation (havis) for Kuñcika,
consisting of two small portions of rice cooked with milk (pāyasa), which is superior to all other wealth.
Having distributed [the offerings] according to the proper rite, one should perform the *śrāddha* with reverence,
providing seats, water for rinsing the feet, drinks, and various garments.
One should give to the guru the water for rinsing, the vessels used for food, all the ritual implements, the entire set of offerings, and the ground.
It should be given to those who stand in the place of a guru, or to those of one's own lineage, or again to the Kaulikas;
but it should never be given to the bound souls (paśus).
Beginning from the time of death, for one month or for ten days,
one should perform a sacrifice (yāga) every day, conjoined with the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjā).
On the first day of the month or on the twelfth day,
the Yoginīs and the Yogins should be respectfully invoked at dawn by one who possesses a beautiful brother, with arms outstretched.
Having washed his feet, offer [the water] until the end;
having worshipped him for the sake of Śivabhairava with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth.
Having offered the apūpa and the vegetable dish along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of peace,
and having set aside the common vessels separately from those of the preceptor;
Having honored the divine [deity] with meat, fish, rice, and other offerings,
and having provided side dishes along with the sacrificial post (yūpa), one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's own capacity.
18a) Then,
at the conclusion of the Yoginī-cakra worship,
one should place a flask filled with divine substances situated in the midst of śāli rice.
Having wrapped it with two garments, one should deposit the nine jewels,
along with the ninefold self and the [nine] consorts beginning with Vaśinī.
Having also invoked [the deity] with the root mantra, one should place a vessel made of gold,
silver, or even glass above and deposit the [substances] therein.
Having established the Lord of the Ninefold Self within the water contained in the pitcher,
one should meditate upon the deceased there and worship him with flowers and other offerings.
A lamp-vessel made from rice flour twelve finger-breadths in size should be placed upon that plate by one intent on the practice, using this mantra.
O Supreme Goddess, having lit a lamp with cow’s ghee and having meditated upon the form of the Vidyā for the sake of the goal, one should then proceed with this mantra.
The ladder for ascending to heaven, the flight of stairs for climbing to the celestial realm,
she is the foremost among those who attain the divine state of moving through the sky.
Having thus recited the mantra, one should cause [the disciple], who embodies the thirty-six principles (tattvas),
to ascend the ladder and lead him upward in due order.
Having dissolved the earth principle up to the level of the Śiva-principle,
one [rests] in the supreme abode beyond the principles, whose form is light and bliss.
One should unite with that consciousness which is free from conceptual construction and devoid of appearance;
having prostrated before the circle of Yoginīs, this rite shall become supreme.
Having made this request, one should gratify the assembly of yoginīs with wine and other offerings.
She should keep a vigil at night together with Nanda and his Kaula companions;
in the morning, she should perform the worship of the Cakra preceded by the rite of the Full Self.
Having placed the turmeric in a mortar, the mantra-versed [practitioner],
together with the Yoginīs, should grind it into powder using the root mantra.
One should not offer [the offering] at the feet of the Guru or the Deity;
rather, one should place it upon the head of each of the Bhairavas and the Śaktis individually.
One should worship the circle of yoginīs for the sake of the ācārya with ritual fees;
having prostrated and made a request, one should first present the image and other offerings.
For as long as a year, one should constantly worship a single Śakti;
or for three months, or until death, or for a year at the end of a vow.
One should worship the circle of yoginīs with fish, meat, rice, and other offerings;
for a full year, performing both external and internal worship.
Having performed all the sequential rites, one should effect the union within that which transcends reality, higher than the highest,
devoid of appearance, stainless, and peaceful.

Therefore, one should act in this manner every year, or perhaps at the time of the lunar mansions or the funeral offerings, for those who are destitute of knowledge of their lineage and are overcome by the fear of saṃsāra.
Before death,
having recognized one's own kinsmen or those of equal status, one should diligently honor the teacher and the elders for the sake of purification.
Having honored him with wealth, grain, and other gifts, I joined my palms in reverence.
O Lord of Gods, O God, having accepted your own splendor for protection,
be gracious to me, O Protector, and thus grant my request as I petition you.
Except in the case of an ignorant man who has died of disease, his daughter may be married to one born of her own lineage;
having performed the pacification of his own [lineage], O Brahmin, he should cause the marriage ceremony to be performed.
Beginning from the collection of the corpse until the end of the entire year,
this is common to all according to the view of Karmavāpyaṣṭika.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the sequence of the final investigation of reality; it is complete.

According to the system of Subhagānandanātha, it is impossible to say whether this eighteenth chapter was spoken by Īśvara or composed by a teacher at some point; rather, even a practitioner, having performed reflection, should carry out the rituals and so forth.
May there be auspiciousness in the year 1929.
